title: The world is not linear extrapolation: be the important variable in the game
dek: If the world ran on logical deduction, today's biggest recommendation engine company would be Baidu. Xiao Hong says what a founder must do is not deduce the inevitable, but make themselves the variable that changes the outcome of the game.
why: The most valuable part of this three-hour interview is the second half: Agent product architecture, model capability spillover, why DeepSeek won. The first-half startup retrospective can be fast-forwarded.
who: AI application founders, heads of product going overseas, investors watching the Agent space; especially suited to teams currently agonizing over whether to build a model, and whether to build an Agent.
skip: The rapid-fire Q&A starting at 3:03 and the first startup retrospective from 5:15-33:16 can be fast-forwarded; the second half is worth more.

points.h: VC's expensiveness doesn't show when you're doing badly
points.body: Xiao Hong defines capital as a tool, and an extremely expensive means of raising money. The mechanism he gives: VC's expensiveness doesn't show when you're doing badly — under the terms, orthodox American financing doesn't have to be repaid — it shows when you're doing well, when you're killing it, the price you pay is bigger. From this he derives his read on a competitor: that company raised more money, so it must deliver a bigger story to its investors, and is therefore forced into doing the wrong things. His conclusion is that even if what you end up doing is smaller, it's far better than doing the wrong thing, and a CEO should have the courage to do the right but small thing.

points.h: Reading the platform: plugins will inevitably be killed off
points.body: When WeCom opened its interfaces, Xiao Hong judged that plugins would inevitably be cleaned up by the platform, but nobody knew when. His reasoning: if you only think about customers, of course customers want to send as many ads as possible; but if you think about the platform, you know the WeChat ecosystem can't be allowed to descend into chaos, and Tencent will definitely restrict it. So the key move isn't to wait until plugins get killed off and then start building, but to work ahead of time — because building an SCRM tool takes at least a month, and by the time that day comes it's too late to start. He distills it into a reusable principle: when facing something you're almost certain will happen but don't know when, the earlier you prepare within the range of costs you can bear, the better.

points.h: While Jasper celebrated its expansion, he saw the cracks
points.body: Xiao Hong studied Jasper, the most successful company running on the GPT-3 API, and saw its founder write an open letter celebrating growth from 9 people to over 200. His judgment was the opposite: management itself is anti-scale, the more people the more messes, and this company's execution would likely slow down. His second judgment was that Jasper was priced too high, and by the plain common sense of the computer industry, capability and API costs would fall sharply, so a market skewed toward individuals and professionals rather than enterprise procurement should emerge. Third, after ChatGPT came out he confirmed that conversational was the general public's imagination of AI. All three together made him decide to launch Monica before ChatGPT was even released, with an internal goal of just 5,000 RMB a month in revenue.

points.h: Bought growth teaches the team nothing
points.body: After acquiring ChatGPT for Google, Xiao Hong didn't rename it Monica but built a new product instead. The reason wasn't branding but growth feedback: ChatGPT for Google had tens of thousands of new users a day from organic traffic, and if the team just sat on it, a colleague who found a way to bring in 200 new users a day wouldn't feel it was anything special, and the team's rate of learning would slow. By rebuilding Monica, everyone gets excited when they find even a little bit of new growth themselves, and thereby learns how to do growth and operations overseas. At the same time, a bought product is an asset, and funneling traffic to it costs nothing, whereas ad spend is money thrown into the water, which makes people hesitate.

points.h: The Andy-Bill law of the new era
points.body: Xiao Hong uses the semiconductor industry's Andy-Bill law to explain AI: no matter what Andy builds, Bill will eat it. Applied today, model capabilities keep evolving and getting cheaper, but the shell also needs to evolve. Cursor was founded very early, but only became widely known after Cloud 3.5 Sonnet shipped — the rise in model capability brought an iteration in its product capability. Without Cursor, you could still write code with Cloud 3.5 Sonnet inside Claude, but it wouldn't be as smooth. So after model capability spills over, third-party vendors are needed to present the value users can perceive, and that's the part founders can define.

points.h: Surfacing the thinking process is an experience innovation
points.body: Xiao Hong believes DeepSeek's global explosion wasn't just about technical strength, but about presenting technical innovations in a way users can perceive. He cites the Publicity CEO's point: in the AI era there are two huge experience innovations, one is marking citation sources when answering with web access, the other is showing the LM's thinking process. OpenAI's o1 actually thinks too, but o1 charges money and only shows a simplified version, and many people simply don't know this exists, so it missed this experience innovation. DeepSeek is free, shows it in full, and on top of that its model quality really reached the first tier, so even friends back in his hometown can feel the generational difference.

points.h: An Agent should write its own code and call APIs
points.body: Xiao Hong describes the moment he was struck by lightning: using Windsurf's Yolo mode, the Agent said it was going to GitHub to pull code, do something, and then write. He realized it was actually using tools. From this he derives the Agent's architecture: a virtual server, a browser, able to write its own code and call APIs. Because much of human knowledge and many services are invoked not through APIs but through the web, it must carry a browser; because it needs to execute command lines and install libraries, it needs a virtual machine in the cloud, and it doesn't matter if it breaks, it can be released when the task ends. He also points out that Yolo mode making users fill in yes is passing the buck — a novice user has no idea what yes or no means.

points.h: Think in terms of games, not logical deduction
points.body: Xiao Hong distinguishes two ways of thinking: logical deduction is ‘Baidu has the best algorithm engineers, so Baidu will definitely nail recommendations’; game thinking is that because you appear and other players appear, the whole environment is different. He gives examples: without this DeepSeek wave, nobody would be thinking about open source; if the original ChatGPT had been built by a third-party company, OpenAI might have chosen to be a pure platform company rather than a consumer app company. His previous startup doing WeCom CRM was the same — because someone in the ecosystem was doing it very well, WeCom said it would leave it to the ecosystem. So founders should try as hard as possible to make themselves that important variable.

terms.def: No matter what Andy (Intel) builds, Bill (Microsoft) will eat it — hardware capability is ultimately consumed by software.
A model's ability to plan over long horizons, solve problems step by step, and call tools, as distinct from resolving things in a single round of conversation.
You only look once — the Agent automatically executes operations like fixing errors, no longer asking the user to confirm step by step.
Product-Market Fit; Xiao Hong says it's like math, if you don't have it you don't have it.
The complex-task benchmark mentioned when Deep Research launched, requiring multi-step reasoning and tool calls.

quotes.text: But the expensiveness doesn't show when you're doing badly. Its expensiveness shows when you're doing well, when you're killing it, the price you pay is bigger.

You're facing something you're almost certain will happen — which is, plugins will be killed off — you think it will definitely happen, but you don't know when. What can you do? Within the range of costs you can bear, the earlier you prepare for it, the better.

In the AI era there are two huge experience innovations. One is that if you're connected to the web, it can answer with the web, and it marks out which webpage each sentence is cited from — that makes people trust it more, right, increases the credibility of the result, having a source. Yes, having a source. The second huge experience innovation he mentioned is showing the LM's thinking process.

If the world ran on logical deduction, today's biggest recommendation engine company would be Baidu. So first, it is not logical deduction — knowing that, I think, is already very important for everyone. Second, try as hard as possible to make yourself an important variable. Third, how do you try as hard as possible? There's no way — you can only be yourself.
